aegis.role: Solo project · product, front, back and security
aegis.summary: A security posture scanner for domains. It checks TLS, HTTP headers, cookies, DNS and email, known vulnerabilities in the detected technologies, reputation and attack surface, then gives a score from 0 to 100 with what to fix.
highlights: Cross-references the detected technologies with OSV, NVD and the CISA KEV catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities.
Passive by default. Active tests only run after the owner proves domain ownership (TXT record or file), with an HMAC token and no database.
The scanner itself is hardened: SSRF protection that revalidates the IP on every connection (anti DNS rebinding), ReDoS-free detection and API rate limiting.
aegis.alt: Aegis dashboard: security score, TLS certificate and checks for a domain

bumphub.role: Solo project · architecture, front, back, desktop and security
bumphub.usage: In production with the company's IT team.
bumphub.summary: Internal workspace for the IT team at Bump Amortecedores. It brings together real-time chat, task management, GitHub integration, an inventory of the company's machines and a password vault, all in its own desktop app.
highlights: Discord-style real-time chat (channels, DMs, mentions, reactions, attachments) with GitHub PR and issue cards right in the conversation.
Inventory of the company's PCs with online/offline status and one-click remote access, plus a maintenance history for each machine.
Password vault encrypted in the browser (AES-256) with 2FA/TOTP: not even the database can see the passwords.
bumphub.alt: BUMPHUB login screen (sign in with GitHub)

about.title: About me
about.heading: I learn by building. And I build to understand.
body: I'm Leonardo, a full-stack developer focused on security. I learned by doing: building projects, breaking things and digging into why they break. Today I work in development, but cybersecurity is where I direct my studies and my career.
At Bump Amortecedores, I run internal pentests every week, do QA, code review and fixes via Pull Request, and I single-handedly built BumpHub, the IT team's internal workspace.

problem.title: The problem
body: Assessing a domain's security means pulling together dozens of checks and sources: certificate, headers, DNS, email, known vulnerabilities, blocklists, forgotten subdomains.
Aegis does it in a single scan and tells you what to fix.

groups.label: TLS
groups.items: Certificate validity and chain, accepted versions (1.0 to 1.3), weak ciphers, key size, signature algorithm, OCSP stapling.

groups.label: Transport and headers
groups.items: HTTP→HTTPS redirect, HSTS, CSP, clickjacking, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, server version disclosure, security.txt.

groups.label: Cookies
groups.items: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite.

groups.label: DNS and email
groups.items: SPF (including the 10-lookup limit), DMARC (including inherited), DKIM, MTA-STS, TLS-RPT, CAA, DNSSEC.

groups.label: Vulnerabilities
groups.items: Detected technologies cross-referenced with OSV, NVD and CISA KEV.

groups.label: Reputation
groups.items: Spamhaus, SURBL and, optionally, Google Safe Browsing and URLhaus.

groups.label: Attack surface
groups.items: Subdomains via Certificate Transparency (crt.sh, Cert Spotter) and HackerTarget, with detection of subdomain takeover, internal IPs in public DNS and sensitive subdomains.

groups.label: Active tests (only with proof of ownership)
groups.items: Exposed sensitive files (.env, .git, backups, admin panels) and internal service ports.

score.title: How the score works
body: A weighted average of the checks: a pass counts for its full weight, a warn for half.
Serious findings cap the score, no matter how good the rest is:

ethics.title: Ethical by design
body: Scanning ports or probing for files on third-party sites without authorization is a crime (in Brazil, Law 12.737/2012). That's why active tests require proof of ownership: a TXT record at _aegis-verify.<domain> or a file at /.well-known/aegis-verify.txt, with an HMAC token for the domain.
On a CDN or shared hosting, the port scan is skipped: that IP serves other customers.

self.title: Securing Aegis itself
items: SSRF: rejects private IPs and revalidates the IP on connect and on every redirect.
A time budget per scan (45 s) and a size limit on external responses.
Rate limit of 30 req/min per IP on Vercel Firewall.

arch.title: Architecture
body: No accounts and no database: history lives in the browser's localStorage and can be exported as JSON.
No dependencies besides lucide-react: the globe is Canvas 2D and the charts are SVG.

flow.label: Scanner
flow.note: checks with a 45 s budget, anti-SSRF

flow.label: External sources
flow.note: DNS, TLS, OSV, NVD, KEV, CT, blocklists

next.title: Limitations and next steps
items: Possible false positives on server CVEs, because distros backport fixes (the advertised version doesn't change).

security.title: Security
items: Row Level Security on every table, with an allowlist: anyone not cleared can't read anything.
Direct messages visible only to their participants.
Password vault encrypted in the browser (AES-256) with 2FA/TOTP: not even the database can see the passwords.
The official server only accepts the desktop app, as an extra layer.
Secrets only in environment variables, never in the repository.

result.title: Outcome
items: In production with the IT team.
Desktop app released through GitHub Releases.
Continuous deployment, with a preview for every pull request.
